problem: Real-world ObjectNav is usually treated as a single end-to-end policy, or over-relies on VLMs for fine-grained exploration. VLMs have weak 3D spatial grounding, so this causes backtracking, inefficiency and poor real-robot transfer, especially at building scale and across embodiments.
motivation: Real-world ObjectNav combines complex spatial structure, long-horizon planning and semantic understanding, and real-robot training data is scarce. VLMs offer commonsense priors (e.g. refrigerator in kitchen) but lack spatial consistency, so they should be used only at the level where they are strong: choosing rooms.
key_idea: Decouple ObjectNav into semantic reasoning, room-based navigation planning and embodiment-specific motion control, using a three-layer room/viewpoint/object scene graph so the VLM only makes room-level decisions while classical exploration covers each room.
insight: VLM reasoning is best restricted to room-level decisions, with efficient classical exploration within rooms. This gives a large real-world efficiency and success gain over VLFM and InstructNav (hard setting SR 98.3 vs 37.2/25.6). No ablation is reported, so the evidence is comparative only. The authors note that their stricter coverage strategy gives smaller SPL gains than SR gains in simulation.
method: Room node construction: fit wall planes and analyse the z-axis point-cloud distribution, dilate the walls to split space into disconnected rooms, and store each room's mask, category and best-view image.

Viewpoint nodes: add a viewpoint (with panorama) when the current coverage adds more than epsilon novel voxels beyond the union of existing coverage regions within d_cover, so images are stored compactly.

Object nodes and edges: open-vocabulary detection and segmentation (YOLOv8x-worldv2 + SAM2.1) with LiDAR give 3D instances. Attributes (color, etc.) and object-object spatial relations are inferred on demand by the VLM from stored images. Room-room, room-viewpoint, room-object and viewpoint-object edges complete the graph.

In-room exploration: a TARE-style two-level (local and global) planner that samples pose candidates in the room mask by uncovered-surface coverage score, solves a TSP, keeps the minimum-cost of K repeats, and uses a rolling window.

Cross-room navigation with VLM (Gemini-2.5-flash): in early-stop mode it decides whether to abandon the current room when a new room is discovered. In room-query mode, after a room is finished, it selects the most likely uncovered room from room attributes, trajectory and goal.
Low-level base autonomy: a waypoint-following, collision-avoidance and terrain-traversability stack with wheeled, Go2 and G1 motion control modules (built-in locomotion policies for legged robots).

setting.backbone: Gemini-2.5-flash (frozen) for VLM reasoning; YOLOv8x-worldv2 + SAM2.1 hiera_b+ for detection/segmentation
setting.observation: 360° panoramic RGB + LiDAR point cloud (real); 640x480 RGB-D + pose in simulation
setting.action_space: continuous velocity via waypoints (real); discrete forward 0.25 m / turn 30° in Habitat
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D-v1, HM3D-v2, MP3D, HM3D-OVON) plus real world
setting.privileged: none (robot pose used in simulation as in the Habitat setup)

numbers.eval_set_note: 48 episodes, wheeled robot, three rooms, cross-room

numbers_note: Simulation split names (HM3D-v1/v2, MP3D) are not stated explicitly; 'val' is assumed. The text says 'SR and SPL improve 14.1% and 6.5%' on HM3D-OVON. There is no ablation table.
results: SysNav reaches SR 63.7 on HM3D-v1, 80.8 on HM3D-v2, 50.7 on MP3D and 54.9 (SPL 26.1) on HM3D-OVON, beating ApexNav on SR (59.6/76.2/39.2) and MTU3D on OVON (40.8). Its SPL is slightly below ApexNav on HM3D-v1 and v2. In 112 real-world episodes it gets 98-100% SR versus at most 58.3% for VLFM and 55.0% for InstructNav, and is a few times faster in the hard setting.
limitations: No ablations isolating the room-level VLM, the scene representation or the in-room exploration.
Stricter coverage causes over-coverage in simulation, giving lower SPL than ApexNav on HM3D.
Quantitative real-world evaluation is on the wheeled robot only, with three environments and a relatively small number of episodes.
